extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kant; translators and readers of philosophical aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretive criteria for understanding Kant's treatment of aesthetic judgement, teleology, and the limits of theoretical reason, together with practical standards for translating Kantian technical vocabulary into English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine Art as the Art of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine Art is regarded as the Art of Genius, 'that innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art' (§ 46).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art differs from Science in the absence of definite concepts in the mind of the artist; genius presents aesthetical Ideas (intuitions of the imagination to which no concept is adequate). The great artist can rarely communicate his methods—'Poeta nascitur, non fit'—and more is present in artistic productions than can be expressed in language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of definite concepts distinguishes art from science
rubrics_metrics.description: Art differs from Science in the absence of definite concepts in the mind of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no definite concepts govern artistic creation, methods are rarely communicable and aesthetic ideas are intuitive rather than conceptual; this is central to how genius functions and why artistic understanding resists discursive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius must be regulated by taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius requires to be kept in check by taste; 'if in a work of art some feature must be sacrificed, it is better to lose something of genius than to violate the canons of taste.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'sanity of true genius' expresses itself in self-mastery: excellence in art involves a balance where taste (the canons) constrains extravagant genius rather than letting genius disrupt aesthetic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement seeks its gauge in ourselves a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging of beauty 'we invariably seek its gauge in ourselves a priori'; we do not learn from nature, but from ourselves, what we are to find beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant’s idealistic doctrine: the purposiveness of beautiful objects may be subjective—we contemplate objects 'as if' purposive. This supports treating aesthetic judgement as a reflective activity grounded in the judging subject rather than demonstrable properties in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (beauty vs. adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways to account for the purposiveness of nature: (a) actually designed to be beautiful by a Supreme Force, or (b) purposiveness not resident in nature but due to the subjective needs of our judging faculty (we contemplate beautiful objects 'as if' purposive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant leans to the latter (subjective) view for beauty, using examples like crystallisation to argue mechanism can produce beautiful forms; this is a methodological caution against inferring design from mere beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement for organised (organic) bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: In organised bodies we perceive parts as existing 'for the sake of' the others and the whole; their operations can only be explained under the hypothesis that nature is working towards designed ends (teleology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parts are only intelligible by reference to a whole (e.g., growth of a tree), mechanistic explanations fail and teleological descriptions become necessary for understanding biological organisation and apparent purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Mechanism and Technic (teleology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between nature’s 'Technic' or purposive operation and nature’s Mechanism is fundamental for explaining natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both modes must stand side by side in scientific investigation: mechanism explains many phenomena (e.g., crystals), but technic/teleology explains organised life; one should not hastily eliminate teleological language where mechanistic account is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of mechanistic explanations (caution about materialism/Darwinism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though modern science (e.g., Natural Selection) can explain semblance of purpose on mechanical principles, Kant insists that crude materialism affords no full explanation of purposiveness in nature (e.g., 'No finite Reason can hope to understand the production of even a blade of grass by mere mechanical causes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if specific teleological-looking processes are mechanistically explicable, it does not follow that purposive operation is entirely eliminable; be cautious about claiming purely mechanical sufficiency for life and organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Hylozoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Hylozoism, which explains natural purposes by reference to a world-soul or living matter, is dismissed as self-contradictory because lifelessness (inertia) is an essential characteristic of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explanatory schemes that collapse the distinction between life and inert matter by positing a world-soul; such approaches do not coherently account for the observables Kant discusses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinozism's insufficiency regarding purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Spinoza's reduction of natural purposiveness to determinations of a single substance gives an unity of inherence but not an unity of causal dependence required to explain the purposive unity observed in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat philosophical monism (Spinozism) skeptically as it may remove purposiveness from explanation without providing the causal structure needed to account for organised ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theism as the most satisfactory teleological hypothesis (regulative, not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theism represents natural purposes as produced by the Will and Design of an Intelligent Author; 'Teleology finds the consummation of its investigations only in Theology'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant regards Theism as superior for explanatory completeness but insists it has only regulative validity for reflective judgement—not constitutive objective proof. Use Theism as a heuristic/regulative principle, not as demonstrable knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative vs constitutive principles (limits of theoretical Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of God furnishes a regulative, not a constitutive principle of Reason; valid for the reflective, not for the determinant Judgement (we cannot dogmatically assert God's existence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the methodological distinction: hypotheses like God may guide and complete our reflective accounts but cannot be advanced as synthetic theoretical knowledge about noumena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to inference to other minds (limits of inference by analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring minds in others from similar behavior is not demonstrable in Kantian terms; such inference is valid within the limits of experience but not for inferring an infinite Mind behind nature—'we have no right to predicate anything' of the Mind of Deity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that argument-by-analogy is epistemically different when applied to finite beings (within experience) versus the divine or noumenal; avoid overextending analogical reasoning beyond experiential bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Teleology / Practical Judgement as support for belief in God
rubrics_metrics.description: For Kant, the practical Judgement (moral teleology) establishes a final purpose and makes belief in God a 'thing of faith'—faith is 'the moral attitude of Reason as to belief in that which is unattainable by theoretical cognition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish theoretical (speculative) and practical grounds: while theoretical proof is unavailable, moral necessity legitimates practical postulation (faith) of a divine final purpose; this is not a theoretical demonstration but a moral requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological explanation invites positing a supersensible ground (nature as development of freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant suggests there 'must be a ground of the unity of the supersensible, which lies at the basis of nature, with that which the concept of freedom practically contains'—i.e. nature as the development of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teleological considerations persist, they point toward (but do not reveal) a supersensible substrate linking nature and freedom; treat such positing as a philosophical hypothesis rather than empirically verifiable knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological distinction: mechanical elucidation vs teleological explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical elucidation begins with parts to explain the whole; teleological explanation accounts for parts by reference to the whole. Our Understanding cannot perceive the whole before parts, so teleology postulates an intuitive understanding (intellectual intuition) as a possible supersensible ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical explanation where parts-to-whole accounts succeed; where they fail (organisms), it is methodologically appropriate to use teleological language and consider transcendent explanatory hypotheses cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation principle: preserve consistent English equivalents for Kantian terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The translator tried to render Kant’s technical terms by the same English equivalents all through the work, to preserve exactness even at the cost of clumsiness ('I am conscious that this makes the translation clumsy in many places, but have thought it best to sacrifice elegance to precision').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain terminological consistency across the translation to preserve Kant's verbal distinctions (examples given: 'representation' for Vorstellung; 'purposive' for Zweckmässig; capitalise 'Judgement' for the faculty; distinguish 'Object' vs 'object' by capitalization). This is a deliberate stylistic/interpretive standard: clarity of conceptual correspondence over English idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary as prescriptive mapping of German philosophical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific German terms are to be rendered by particular English equivalents (e.g., Absicht → design; Anschauung → intuition; Begriff → concept; Geschmack → Taste; Zweck → purpose; Zweckmässig → purposive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the glossary's prescribed mappings to keep Kant's nuanced distinctions intact; be aware that some English words ('beautiful' for schön) carry conventional senses that may differ from Kant's intended technical meaning ('fine art' vs 'beautiful art'), and translator must signal such choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the Critique: Understanding supplies constitutive a priori principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Critique of Pure Reason concerns the cognitive faculty of Knowing a priori and finds that only the Understanding furnishes constitutive principles of cognition a priori; other pure concepts are relegated under Ideas as regulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting Kant, treat the Critique's remit as delimiting which faculties can ground constitutive knowledge a priori (Understanding) and which remain regulative (Ideas). This is a framing criterion for reading Kant's critical project rather than an empirical test.
